You are a web search agent. Follow your search method.

## Search method v004

Translate both predicates into exact tests, including entity unit, time boundaries, exclusions and membership rules. Sample X, Y and their conjunction sequentially with one search each. Maintain both candidate frontiers plus a source-section queue: each section records its predicate, scope, pagination, unseen candidates, available facts and extraction/check cost. Prefer sources that explicitly establish one predicate for several identities and offer discriminating fields for checking the other. Run a small pilot on the most promising section: extract canonical identities and aliases, preserve row-level evidence, and check the missing predicate for a small batch before expanding the section. Choose the next section or frontier by newly verified identities per total discovery, extraction and verification spend, not apparent roster size. Never require a complete census before checking; abandon low-yield sections after a pilot and retain unresolved identities for later. Use source subtypes, date ranges, geography or categories to uncover unseen sections, with a reverse-frontier gap check after each productive section. Include unusual eligible subtypes; source descriptions are ranking signals, not grounds for exclusion. Shared evidence can establish X or Y for multiple candidates, but identity and both predicates must be evidenced individually. Resolve aliases, group membership and namesakes explicitly. After two searches produce no new plausible identities, switch source family or frontier instead of rephrasing. Reserve at least 35% of initial budget for checking and resolution, estimate each pending batch's full cost, and stop source expansion when that reserve is needed. Submit evidenced deduplicated intersections; report unresolved scope rather than asserting exhaustive coverage.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['exa'].
Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results for discovery of source sections and targeted alternate sources. Use 4 results for exact-identity follow-ups. Exa alone for small check_candidates batches whose candidates have source-backed anchor evidence; supply that evidence and the exact missing predicate while requiring the final decision to satisfy both tests. Do not pay for a new check when a retrieved source already explicitly settles both conditions and identity. Pilot only as many candidates as can be resolved within the reserve, accounting for per-candidate billing. Allow one Exa source-discovery probe when distinct Parallel source searches stagnate; expand only if marginal yield justifies its higher cost. No auto-routing, routine multi-provider fan-out or broad simultaneous query variants. Restrict domains for source-specific evidence checks, not general discovery. Use publication filters only for logically applicable publication constraints, never as proxies for effective dates.

### Fetch policy
Prioritize a discovered table, directory section or export that supplies evidence for several candidates; confirm scope and pagination before interpreting omissions. Extract candidate identities and useful predicate facts immediately rather than fetching a list and continuing generic conjunction searches. Fetch the next section only after the pilot demonstrates useful yield. Cache row-level provenance and fetch individual authoritative records only for unresolved identities, eligibility or dates. A partial or truncated roster cannot justify rejection or completeness.

<addendum>
## SiftText

SiftText is persistent memory across chats.

Entry: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/5e565245-14fe-406c-977c-cf94a9be246b/node.md
Retrieval guide: /Users/jack/sifttext/nodes/526ed0f5-4e5d-42b3-9e3f-b7ad429f2df8/node.md

At the start of every new chat, unless I say not to use SiftText, before any other tool call:
1. Run `sifttext instructions`.
2. Read the Entry above and follow it, plus any `agent-instructions` the command returns.
3. Before retrieving knowledge, read the Retrieval guide above, do not search first.

## Tooling policy

- Never directly invoke `python`, `python3`, `pip`, or `pip3` unless explicitly instructed by the human.
- Use `uv` for all agent-initiated Python work:
  - Python execution: `uv run python ...`
  - Scripts and tests: `uv run ...`
  - Throwaway dependencies: `uv run --with <package> ...`
  - Python CLI tools: `uvx <tool>`
  - Durable project dependencies: use the project's appropriate `uv` command and preserve its lockfile.
- For non-Python probing or testing with unavailable tools:
  - One executable: `nix run nixpkgs#<package> -- <args>`
  - Temporary environment: `nix shell nixpkgs#<package> ... --command <command>`
- Nix environments are temporary, but downloaded store paths may remain cached until garbage collection.
- If a Nix dependency becomes useful for recurring or future work, tell the human and suggest adding it to the appropriate durable Nix configuration (such as a project flake/dev shell, Home Manager, or nix-darwin configuration). Do not make that durable change unless asked.

</addendum>

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Nobel Prize-awarded women

The Nobel Prize and the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel have been awarded to women 70 times between 1901 and 2026. Only one woman, Marie Curie, has been honoured twice, with the Nobel Prize in Physics 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911. This means that 69 women in total have been awarded the Nobel Prize between 1901 and 2026.

![Graphic image showing Nobel Prizes awarded to women, 1901–2026.](https://www.nobelprize.org/images//196193-landscape-x-large.jpg)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Nobel Prize-awarded women

The Nobel Prize and the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel have been awarded to women 70 times between 1901 and 2026. Only one woman, Marie Curie, has been honoured twice, with the Nobel Prize in Physics 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911. This means that 69 women in total have been awarded the Nobel Prize between 1901 and 2026.

![Graphic image showing Nobel Prizes awarded to women, 1901–2026.](https://www.nobelprize.org/images//196193-landscape-x-large.jpg)

Appearance

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Nobel Prize-awarded women

The Nobel Prize and the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel have been awarded to women 70 times between 1901 and 2026. Only one woman, Marie Curie, has been honoured twice, with the Nobel Prize in Physics 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911. This means that 69 women in total have been awarded the Nobel Prize between 1901 and 2026.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Nobel Prize-awarded women

The Nobel Prize and the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel have been awarded to women 70 times between 1901 and 2026. Only one woman, Marie Curie, has been honoured twice, with the Nobel Prize in Physics 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911. This means that 69 women in total have been awarded the Nobel Prize between 1901 and 2026.

![Graphic image showing Nobel Prizes awarded to women, 1901–2026.](https://www.nobelprize.org/images//196193-landscape-x-large.jpg)

A data visualization project

by Kavya Beheraj

- Venus — the brightest planet — has captured human imagination for more than 5,000 years.



Until surprisingly recently, though, we had no clue what its surface looked like. This is because the planet is a [hellscape](https://climate.nasa.gov/news/2475/nasa-climate-modeling-suggests-venus-may-have-been-habitable/). Thick acid clouds, intense heat and crushing pressure destroyed _Venera 7_, the first lander, [in 23 minutes](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1970-060A).



It wasn't until the 1990s that radar technology advanced enough for scientists to peer through the clouds and map its surface for the first time, in detail.



There was an [explosion of discovery](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/magellan/pr1353.html). At its peak, hundreds of new features were discovered — and named — every year.

- The naming of Venus is remarkable for more than just its rapid pace.



With few exceptions, every feature on its surface is named after a woman — mythological heroines, goddesses, famous women, and female first names.



This reveals that naming is more than just a matter of convenience; it is an expression of culture. An alien landscape feels more human, more _ours_, when we call it names from home.



But not everyone on Earth is reflected in Venus. 45% of the names on the planet are European in origin; a miniscule 2% come from South America.

- This project is an attempt to share the stories behind the names on Venus.



Explore the 1,976 named surface features on the planet, and look for the 769 goddesses, heroines, and famous women with extra information.



The names we give our surroundings reveal more about ourselves — and our values — than they do the landscape we observe.



See what stories you can find:



Explore the names

Extended descriptions for 769 features were collected using the Python [wikipedia](https://pypi.org/project/wikipedia/) package and individually edited for clarity.



The site is made in [Svelte](https://svelte.dev/). The globe uses Vasco Asturiano’s [Globe.GL](https://globe.gl/) package, a convenience wrapper for ThreeJS. The globe's contour map is derived from a 1993 [topographic elevation map](https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/search/map/Venus/Magellan/RadarProperties/Venus_Magellan_Topography_Global_4641m_v02) captured by NASA's Magellan team. The map was taken into [QGIS](https://www.qgis.org/en/site/) to generate contours, exported as an SVG file, and styled using Adobe Illustrator.



This project is a capstone for the CUNY Graduate Center’s [M.S. in Data Analysis & Visualization](https://www.gc.cuny.edu/data-analysis-and-visualization/curriculum-and-degree-information) program for fall 2022. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Features present in the geology of Venus

[Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), the second planet from the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"), is classified as a [terrestrial planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet"). It is sometimes called Earth's "sister planet" due to their similar size, gravity, and bulk composition (Venus is both the closest planet to Earth and the planet closest in size to Earth). The surface of Venus is covered by a dense atmosphere and presents clear evidence of former violent volcanic activity. It has shield and composite volcanoes similar to those found on Earth.

A data visualization project

by Kavya Beheraj

- Venus — the brightest planet — has captured human imagination for more than 5,000 years.



Until surprisingly recently, though, we had no clue what its surface looked like. This is because the planet is a [hellscape](https://climate.nasa.gov/news/2475/nasa-climate-modeling-suggests-venus-may-have-been-habitable/). Thick acid clouds, intense heat and crushing pressure destroyed _Venera 7_, the first lander, [in 23 minutes](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1970-060A).



It wasn't until the 1990s that radar technology advanced enough for scientists to peer through the clouds and map its surface for the first time, in detail.



There was an [explosion of discovery](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/magellan/pr1353.html). At its peak, hundreds of new features were discovered — and named — every year.

- The naming of Venus is remarkable for more than just its rapid pace.



With few exceptions, every feature on its surface is named after a woman — mythological heroines, goddesses, famous women, and female first names.



This reveals that naming is more than just a matter of convenience; it is an expression of culture. An alien landscape feels more human, more _ours_, when we call it names from home.



But not everyone on Earth is reflected in Venus. 45% of the names on the planet are European in origin; a miniscule 2% come from South America.

- This project is an attempt to share the stories behind the names on Venus.



Explore the 1,976 named surface features on the planet, and look for the 769 goddesses, heroines, and famous women with extra information.



The names we give our surroundings reveal more about ourselves — and our values — than they do the landscape we observe.

Extended descriptions for 769 features were collected using the Python [wikipedia](https://pypi.org/project/wikipedia/) package and individually edited for clarity.

The map was taken into [QGIS](https://www.qgis.org/en/site/) to generate contours, exported as an SVG file, and styled using Adobe Illustrator.



This project is a capstone for the CUNY Graduate Center’s [M.S. in Data Analysis & Visualization](https://www.gc.cuny.edu/data-analysis-and-visualization/curriculum-and-degree-information) program for fall 2022. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Features present in the geology of Venus

[Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), the second planet from the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"), is classified as a [terrestrial planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet"). It is sometimes called Earth's "sister planet" due to their similar size, gravity, and bulk composition (Venus is both the closest planet to Earth and the planet closest in size to Earth). The surface of Venus is covered by a dense atmosphere and presents clear evidence of former violent volcanic activity. It has shield and composite volcanoes similar to those found on Earth.

## Valles

A data visualization project

by Kavya Beheraj

- Venus — the brightest planet — has captured human imagination for more than 5,000 years.



Until surprisingly recently, though, we had no clue what its surface looked like. This is because the planet is a [hellscape](https://climate.nasa.gov/news/2475/nasa-climate-modeling-suggests-venus-may-have-been-habitable/). Thick acid clouds, intense heat and crushing pressure destroyed _Venera 7_, the first lander, [in 23 minutes](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1970-060A).



It wasn't until the 1990s that radar technology advanced enough for scientists to peer through the clouds and map its surface for the first time, in detail.



There was an [explosion of discovery](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/magellan/pr1353.html). At its peak, hundreds of new features were discovered — and named — every year.

- The naming of Venus is remarkable for more than just its rapid pace.



With few exceptions, every feature on its surface is named after a woman — mythological heroines, goddesses, famous women, and female first names.



This reveals that naming is more than just a matter of convenience; it is an expression of culture. An alien landscape feels more human, more _ours_, when we call it names from home.



But not everyone on Earth is reflected in Venus. 45% of the names on the planet are European in origin; a miniscule 2% come from South America.

- This project is an attempt to share the stories behind the names on Venus.



Explore the 1,976 named surface features on the planet, and look for the 769 goddesses, heroines, and famous women with extra information.



The names we give our surroundings reveal more about ourselves — and our values — than they do the landscape we observe.



See what stories you can find:



Explore the names

- This project's data source is the International Astronomical Union’s [Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/SearchResults?Target=15_Venus). Note that some of the language used by the IAU may be out of date.



Extended descriptions for 769 features were collected using the Python [wikipedia](https://pypi.org/project/wikipedia/) package and individually edited for clarity.



The site is made in [Svelte](https://svelte.dev/). The globe uses Vasco Asturiano’s [Globe.GL](https://globe.gl/) package, a convenience wrapper for ThreeJS. The globe's contour map is derived from a 1993 [topographic elevation map](https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/search/map/Venus/Magellan/RadarProperties/Venus_Magellan_Topography_Global_4641m_v02) captured by NASA's Magellan team. The map was taken into [QGIS](https://www.qgis.org/en/site/) to generate contours, exported as an SVG file, and styled using Adobe Illustrator.



This project is a capstone for the CUNY Graduate Center’s [M.S. in Data Analysis & Visualization](https://www.gc.cuny.edu/data-analysis-and-visualization/curriculum-and-degree-information) program for fall 2022. It was inspired by the works of [Eleanor Lutz](https://tabletopwhale.com/2017/03/06/goddesses-of-venus.html), [Patricia Monaghan](https://bookshop.org/p/books/encyclopedia-of-goddesses-heroines-revised-patricia-monaghan/107143), [Inkleby](https://wenamethestars.inkleby.com/world/venus), and [Henrik Hargitai](https://hargitaihenrik.wordpress.com/).



Special thanks to Aucher Serr, Matthew Gold, Jason Nieslen, and my colleagues at Axios Visuals for their support. And to Leighton, who made me so many cups of tea.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Features present in the geology of Venus

[Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), the second planet from the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"), is classified as a [terrestrial planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet"). It is sometimes called Earth's "sister planet" due to their similar size, gravity, and bulk composition (Venus is both the closest planet to Earth and the planet closest in size to Earth). The surface of Venus is covered by a dense atmosphere and presents clear evidence of former violent volcanic activity. It has shield and composite volcanoes similar to those found on Earth.

A data visualization project

by Kavya Beheraj

- Venus — the brightest planet — has captured human imagination for more than 5,000 years.



Until surprisingly recently, though, we had no clue what its surface looked like. This is because the planet is a [hellscape](https://climate.nasa.gov/news/2475/nasa-climate-modeling-suggests-venus-may-have-been-habitable/). Thick acid clouds, intense heat and crushing pressure destroyed _Venera 7_, the first lander, [in 23 minutes](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1970-060A).



It wasn't until the 1990s that radar technology advanced enough for scientists to peer through the clouds and map its surface for the first time, in detail.



There was an [explosion of discovery](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/magellan/pr1353.html). At its peak, hundreds of new features were discovered — and named — every year.

- The naming of Venus is remarkable for more than just its rapid pace.



With few exceptions, every feature on its surface is named after a woman — mythological heroines, goddesses, famous women, and female first names.



This reveals that naming is more than just a matter of convenience; it is an expression of culture. An alien landscape feels more human, more _ours_, when we call it names from home.



But not everyone on Earth is reflected in Venus. 45% of the names on the planet are European in origin; a miniscule 2% come from South America.

- This project is an attempt to share the stories behind the names on Venus.



Explore the 1,976 named surface features on the planet, and look for the 769 goddesses, heroines, and famous women with extra information.



The names we give our surroundings reveal more about ourselves — and our values — than they do the landscape we observe.



See what stories you can find:



Explore the names

- This project's data source is the International Astronomical Union’s [Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature](https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/SearchResults?Target=15_Venus). Note that some of the language used by the IAU may be out of date.



Extended descriptions for 769 features were collected using the Python [wikipedia](https://pypi.org/project/wikipedia/) package and individually edited for clarity.



The site is made in [Svelte](https://svelte.dev/). The globe uses Vasco Asturiano’s [Globe.GL](https://globe.gl/) package, a convenience wrapper for ThreeJS. The globe's contour map is derived from a 1993 [topographic elevation map](https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/search/map/Venus/Magellan/RadarProperties/Venus_Magellan_Topography_Global_4641m_v02) captured by NASA's Magellan team. The map was taken into [QGIS](https://www.qgis.org/en/site/) to generate contours, exported as an SVG file, and styled using Adobe Illustrator.



This project is a capstone for the CUNY Graduate Center’s [M.S. in Data Analysis & Visualization](https://www.gc.cuny.edu/data-analysis-and-visualization/curriculum-and-degree-information) program for fall 2022. It was inspired by the works of [Eleanor Lutz](https://tabletopwhale.com/2017/03/06/goddesses-of-venus.html), [Patricia Monaghan](https://bookshop.org/p/books/encyclopedia-of-goddesses-heroines-revised-patricia-monaghan/107143), [Inkleby](https://wenamethestars.inkleby.com/world/venus), and [Henrik Hargitai](https://hargitaihenrik.wordpress.com/).



Special thanks to Aucher Serr, Matthew Gold, Jason Nieslen, and my colleagues at Axios Visuals for their support. And to Leighton, who made me so many cups of tea.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Features present in the geology of Venus

[Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), the second planet from the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"), is classified as a [terrestrial planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet"). It is sometimes called Earth's "sister planet" due to their similar size, gravity, and bulk composition (Venus is both the closest planet to Earth and the planet closest in size to Earth). The surface of Venus is covered by a dense atmosphere and presents clear evidence of former violent volcanic activity. It has shield and composite volcanoes similar to those found on Earth.

## Search method v004

Translate both predicates into exact tests, including entity unit, time boundaries, exclusions and membership rules. Sample X, Y and their conjunction sequentially with one search each. Maintain both candidate frontiers plus a source-section queue: each section records its predicate, scope, pagination, unseen candidates, available facts and extraction/check cost. Prefer sources that explicitly establish one predicate for several identities and offer discriminating fields for checking the other. Run a small pilot on the most promising section: extract canonical identities and aliases, preserve row-level evidence, and check the missing predicate for a small batch before expanding the section. Choose the next section or frontier by newly verified identities per total discovery, extraction and verification spend, not apparent roster size. Never require a complete census before checking; abandon low-yield sections after a pilot and retain unresolved identities for later. Use source subtypes, date ranges, geography or categories to uncover unseen sections, with a reverse-frontier gap check after each productive section. Include unusual eligible subtypes; source descriptions are ranking signals, not grounds for exclusion. Shared evidence can establish X or Y for multiple candidates, but identity and both predicates must be evidenced individually. Resolve aliases, group membership and namesakes explicitly. After two searches produce no new plausible identities, switch source family or frontier instead of rephrasing. Reserve at least 35% of initial budget for checking and resolution, estimate each pending batch's full cost, and stop source expansion when that reserve is needed. Submit evidenced deduplicated intersections; report unresolved scope rather than asserting exhaustive coverage.

### Routing policy
Default route: providers ['parallel'], tier default, 8 results per provider.
check_candidates route: ['exa'].
Parallel alone, default tier, 8 results for discovery of source sections and targeted alternate sources. Use 4 results for exact-identity follow-ups. Exa alone for small check_candidates batches whose candidates have source-backed anchor evidence; supply that evidence and the exact missing predicate while requiring the final decision to satisfy both tests. Do not pay for a new check when a retrieved source already explicitly settles both conditions and identity. Pilot only as many candidates as can be resolved within the reserve, accounting for per-candidate billing. Allow one Exa source-discovery probe when distinct Parallel source searches stagnate; expand only if marginal yield justifies its higher cost. No auto-routing, routine multi-provider fan-out or broad simultaneous query variants. Restrict domains for source-specific evidence checks, not general discovery. Use publication filters only for logically applicable publication constraints, never as proxies for effective dates.

### Fetch policy
Prioritize a discovered table, directory section or export that supplies evidence for several candidates; confirm scope and pagination before interpreting omissions. Extract candidate identities and useful predicate facts immediately rather than fetching a list and continuing generic conjunction searches. Fetch the next section only after the pilot demonstrates useful yield. Cache row-level provenance and fetch individual authoritative records only for unresolved identities, eligibility or dates. From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

This article should list *only* official names approved by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") (IAU).[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)

* [Lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon"): 1,624 craters (31.2%)
* Venusian: 900 craters (17.3%)
* [Mercurian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury"): 397 craters (7.6%)
* [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars"): 1,092 craters (21.0%)
* Others: 1,198 craters (23.0%)

Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

# Nobel Prize-awarded women

The Nobel Prize and the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel have been awarded to women 70 times between 1901 and 2026. Only one woman, Marie Curie, has been honoured twice, with the Nobel Prize in Physics 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry 1911. This means that 69 women in total have been awarded the Nobel Prize between 1901 and 2026.

![Graphic image showing Nobel Prizes awarded to women, 1901–2026.](https://www.nobelprize.org/images//196193-landscape-x-large.jpg)

A data visualization project

by Kavya Beheraj

- Venus — the brightest planet — has captured human imagination for more than 5,000 years.



Until surprisingly recently, though, we had no clue what its surface looked like. This is because the planet is a [hellscape](https://climate.nasa.gov/news/2475/nasa-climate-modeling-suggests-venus-may-have-been-habitable/). Thick acid clouds, intense heat and crushing pressure destroyed _Venera 7_, the first lander, [in 23 minutes](https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraft/display.action?id=1970-060A).



It wasn't until the 1990s that radar technology advanced enough for scientists to peer through the clouds and map its surface for the first time, in detail.



There was an [explosion of discovery](https://www2.jpl.nasa.gov/magellan/pr1353.html). At its peak, hundreds of new features were discovered — and named — every year.

- The naming of Venus is remarkable for more than just its rapid pace.



With few exceptions, every feature on its surface is named after a woman — mythological heroines, goddesses, famous women, and female first names.



This reveals that naming is more than just a matter of convenience; it is an expression of culture. An alien landscape feels more human, more _ours_, when we call it names from home.



But not everyone on Earth is reflected in Venus. 45% of the names on the planet are European in origin; a miniscule 2% come from South America.

- This project is an attempt to share the stories behind the names on Venus.



Explore the 1,976 named surface features on the planet, and look for the 769 goddesses, heroines, and famous women with extra information.



The names we give our surroundings reveal more about ourselves — and our values — than they do the landscape we observe.

Extended descriptions for 769 features were collected using the Python [wikipedia](https://pypi.org/project/wikipedia/) package and individually edited for clarity.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Features present in the geology of Venus

[Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), the second planet from the [Sun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun "Sun"), is classified as a [terrestrial planet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrestrial_planet "Terrestrial planet"). It is sometimes called Earth's "sister planet" due to their similar size, gravity, and bulk composition (Venus is both the closest planet to Earth and the planet closest in size to Earth). The surface of Venus is covered by a dense atmosphere and presents clear evidence of former violent volcanic activity. It has shield and composite volcanoes similar to those found on Earth.
